description: General technology vocabulary used by src/jobomatic/fit/terms.py to pull skill names out of sentence-style JD bullets (e.g. 'Experience building Azure applications using event-driven architectures' -> Azure, event-driven). Lowercase; matched as whole tokens (a trailing plural 's'/'es' is allowed). Add a term here when a real posting names a technology the parser leaves 'unscored'. Keep ambiguous English words out (no 'go', 'rest', 'r', 'c'). This is the JD-side vocabulary only — whether the candidate has the skill is still decided by src/jobomatic/fit/engine.py against the profile.
category_terms_description: Terms that name a KIND of tool, not a product. In 'NoSQL databases such as MongoDB' the requirement is the category, and MongoDB only illustrates it, so the category and its examples are scored as one entry met by evidence for either. Only these terms join their examples; a product ('Python libraries such as Pandas') does not, or having Python alone would meet it. Every term must also be in 'terms'.
umbrella_terms_description: Terms so broad that the word alone is easy to match (any project that mentions AI). When examples follow one ('AI-assisted tools such as Copilot, Claude Code, or Cursor'), the umbrella is dropped and the examples carry the requirement; joined to them, it would let any AI project meet it. A requirement that is only the umbrella is scored as usual. Every term must also be in 'terms' and may not also be a category term.
umbrellas_description: Umbrella skills scored by their parts (ADR 0022). A requirement that is only the umbrella ('Experience with AI') is met by the best evidence among the parts, never by the bare word; the fit table names the part that earned the status. The parts are the owner's to define. A string value means 'the same parts as that umbrella'. Keys must be umbrella terms; every part must be in 'terms'.
phrase_expansions_description: A phrase that stands for two or more skills at once ('AI-assisted automation' is AI, and workflow automation). Written lower case with hyphens as spaces; the value lists the terms it expands to, each of which must be in 'terms'. Edit freely.
caps_only_description: Terms that are also ordinary English words and count as a skill only when the posting writes them in capitals: 'Solid understanding of CI/CD' is an adjective, 'SOLID principles' is the skill. Every term must also be in 'terms'.
list_only_description: Terms that are also ordinary English words and count as a skill only when written with a capital first letter, directly next to another vocabulary term in a list ('Java, Go, GraphQL', 'Go or Rust'). 'Go' alone, or 'go to market', is not the language. Every term must also be in 'terms'.
kind_nouns_description: Terms that name a KIND of tool and, written right after a more specific term, add nothing: 'OAuth authentication' asks for OAuth, not OAuth and authentication. On their own they still count ('Experience with authentication'). Every term must also be in 'terms'.
or_other_description: 'or other <kind>' after a tool of an alternatives group means any tool of that group meets the requirement: 'AWS, or other cloud platforms' is scored as 'AWS / Azure / GCP / Google Cloud'. Each key is a group name from 'alternative_groups'; each value lists the phrases that name that kind of tool. Keep to phrases that name the whole group: not 'languages' or 'frameworks'.
alternative_groups_description: Terms in the same group are interchangeable choices of one kind of tool: when a requirement joins two or more of them with '/' or 'or' ("Entity Framework/ Dapper", "AWS or Azure"), any one meets it, so they are scored as ONE entry ('A / B'). Joined with 'and', or from different groups ('C#/.NET'), they stay separate requirements. Every term must also be in 'terms', and a term may belong to one group only. Keep a group to tools a posting treats as one skill when it writes them with '/' or 'or' (the owner's call: 'Agile/Scrum' and 'JavaScript/TypeScript' are each one row, while 'Agile and Scrum' stays two). Not 'html'/'css', which postings ask for together.
